title: POGs: The 90s in a Bottle Cap
summary: Josh and Chuck explore POGs, the 1990s collectible cardboard discs fad. They trace the game's roots to milk caps played by Hawaiian schoolchildren (introduced by teacher Blossom Galbiso in the early 1990s), which descended from the Japanese card game Manko, brought to Hawaii by immigrants. Milk caps came from a Hawaiian dairy whose Passion Orange Guava (POG) drink gave the game its name. Marketer Alan Rapinski bought the POG brand, formed the World Pog Federation, and licensed POGs to businesses and promotions, leading to a saturated market, school bans, and a decline attributed partly to the O.J. Simpson slammer and fads aging out. The episode explains the gameplay (stacking, slammers, keeping face-up discs, poison pogs, regional rule variations). The closing segment covers US military Army and Air Force Exchange Service cardboard POG coins used as currency in Afghanistan from 2001, and a listener mail about slime molds.

segments.title: Intro and POG fad overview
segments.summary: The hosts introduce POGs as a flash-in-the-pan 1990s fad that was both a trading craze and a game, and note the Simpsons reference and Jesse Thorn's enthusiasm.

segments.title: Blossom Galbiso and milk caps
segments.summary: A Hawaiian teacher and guidance counselor, Blossom Galbiso, introduced her students to milk caps, an older game played with cardboard bottle caps, to replace dangerous dodgeball. Kids then asked the dairy and packager Stampac for more caps.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short sponsor read for Stampac and a break.

segments.title: Name origin: Passion Orange Guava and Manko
segments.summary: The name POG comes from the Hawaiian dairy's Passion Orange Guava drink, whose caps were used for the game. The game descends from the Japanese card game Manko, brought to Hawaii by Japanese immigrants, with milk caps replacing cards and stacks replacing single flips.

segments.title: Alan Rapinski and the World Pog Federation
segments.summary: Marketer Alan Rapinski, known for Armor All, spotted the trend and bought the POG brand from the dairy, forming the World Pog Federation to license POGs. Licensed promotions by fast food chains, the Pope, and others followed, and knockoffs saturated the market.

segments.title: Sponsor break and plug
segments.summary: Break with a plug for a pulp fiction episode.

segments.title: How to play POGs and school bans
segments.summary: Gameplay explained: a stack of POGs is slammed with a heavier slammer, and face-up discs are kept. Playing for keeps caused fights and gambling concerns, leading schools and several countries to ban POGs. Variations include poison POGs and regional rules.

segments.title: Decline of POGs and dairy's missed opportunity
segments.summary: POGs faded as school bans, aging out, and the O.J. Simpson slammer contributed to the decline. The Hawaiian dairy did not benefit financially and was left out of the fad.

segments.title: Military POG coins in Afghanistan
segments.summary: The Army and Air Force Exchange Service issued cardboard POG-style coins from November 2001 for use as currency by American service members in Afghanistan, cheaper to ship than metal coins, until recently.
topics: Army and Air Force Exchange Service

segments.title: Listener mail: slime molds and outro
segments.summary: A listener writes about slime molds, which he gives away and breeds, and a microscopist reports accidentally tasting one. The episode closes with credits.
